questions.stem: A legal-research firm's deep-research assistant was rebuilt as a lead agent that dispatches parallel subagents. On the firm's internal eval set, answer completeness rose sharply, but the monthly model bill roughly tripled. The CFO, who is not technical, asks the architect to justify the change in the next budget review. Which approach to the conversation is MOST effective?

options.text: Walk the CFO through how the lead agent decomposes each query, how the subagents run in their own context windows, and why that architecture inherently consumes far more tokens per request than a single call.
Commit to bringing the bill back to its old level next quarter by switching every subagent to a smaller model, so the cost concern is closed before the review.

Show cost per completed research memo against the measured quality gain, identify which query types actually need the multi-agent path, and propose routing routine queries to a cheaper single-agent path.
Explain that multi-agent systems are the current industry best practice for research tasks, so the higher cost is the expected price of staying competitive.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder communication should translate an architectural trade-off into business terms (cost per outcome, quality, risk) and offer credible alternatives. Anthropic's multi-agent research write-up notes multi-agent systems use roughly 15x the tokens of a chat interaction and are economically viable only when the task's value justifies that cost. Splitting the traffic so only high-value queries take the expensive path is a defensible, evidence-backed answer to the CFO.

whyWrong.A: Accurate, but it explains the mechanism rather than the business trade-off. A non-technical budget owner needs cost versus value, not context-window internals.
whyWrong.B: It makes a commitment before any eval shows that smaller subagent models keep the quality gain. It trades away the benefit without evidence.
whyWrong.D: An appeal to fashion is not a justification. Anthropic's own guidance is that multi-agent is worth it only when task value is high enough, not that it is always best practice.

questions.mindset: Justify cost with cost-per-outcome and evidence, and offer a cheaper path where the value isn't there.

questions.scenario: An insurance company wants to auto-route incoming customer emails into one of 12 queues. A business sponsor has read about autonomous agent swarms and asks for a multi-agent system in which a planner agent, a classifier agent and a critic agent debate each email before routing it.
questions.stem: In a two-week pilot, a single Claude call with a well-defined category list and a handful of labelled examples already meets the agreed routing-accuracy target and latency budget. What should the architect recommend to the sponsor?

options.text: Recommend the single-call workflow, show the pilot results against the agreed targets, and define the measurable conditions (such as accuracy dropping below target on new email types) that would justify a more complex design.

Build the multi-agent design as requested, since the sponsor owns the budget and has stated a clear preference, and keep the single-call version in reserve as a fallback in case the swarm proves unstable or too slow in production.
Deploy both designs to production behind a traffic split for a quarter so that the sponsor can see real-world results on live email volume before the team commits to either architecture.
Explain to the sponsor that autonomous agents are not yet reliable enough for customer-facing work in general, so the company should standardise on simple prompts for the foreseeable future.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' advises finding the simplest solution that works and adding complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes. The pilot already meets the targets, so the defensible recommendation is the simpler workflow, backed by eval evidence, with explicit criteria for when to reconsider. That respects the sponsor's goal (accurate routing) rather than the proposed mechanism.

whyWrong.B: It builds an over-engineered, more expensive and slower system that adds no measured benefit. Owning the budget does not make an unjustified design defensible.
whyWrong.C: The pilot has already answered the question against the agreed targets, and the swarm doesn't exist yet. Building and running two production systems for a quarter spends real engineering and operating effort to re-learn what the eval already shows.
whyWrong.D: It is an overgeneralisation that the evidence doesn't support, and it closes off agentic designs even where they might later be warranted.

questions.mindset: Recommend the simplest design that meets the agreed targets, and name the trigger for adding complexity.

questions.stem: Eight months after launch, a new engineering manager asks why the team chose retrieval over the document store instead of fine-tuning, and nobody who was in the original meetings is still on the project. Which practice would have BEST preserved this reasoning?

options.text: Saving the slide deck from the original design review in the team's shared drive and linking it from the project's onboarding page so that new joiners can find and read it.
Adding detailed code comments in the retrieval module that describe how chunks are fetched, ranked, filtered and inserted into the prompt before each model call.
Keeping the full Slack thread in which the options were debated pinned in the project channel, with a note telling new joiners to read it before changing anything.
Writing an architecture decision record that captures the context, the options considered, the decision, its consequences and the conditions that would prompt a revisit.

questions.explanation: A decision record (ADR) is the standard artifact for communicating why a choice was made. In the widely used Nygard format it states the context and constraints, the decision, its status and its consequences, and good practice adds the alternatives weighed and when to reconsider. It is short, versioned alongside the code and findable, so the rationale outlives the people who made the decision. Claude Code's own guidance treats architectural decisions as something to record in the project's shared, version-controlled instructions for the same reason. This is general architecture practice that the Professional path expects you to apply to Claude solutions.

whyWrong.A: Review slides usually show the conclusion and the winning design in detail but compress or omit the rejected alternatives and the trade-offs; they also go stale and get lost in shared drives.
whyWrong.B: Code comments explain how the code works, not why this approach beat the alternatives.
whyWrong.C: A long discussion thread is hard to search, mixes early ideas with the final decision and doesn't record consequences or revisit triggers.

questions.mindset: Record why, not just what: context, options, decision, consequences, revisit triggers.

questions.stem: An architect is presenting a steering committee of business executives with a choice between a fixed, step-by-step document-processing workflow and a more autonomous agent that decides its own steps. The committee must approve one option this week. Which TWO elements will MOST help the committee make a sound decision? Choose TWO.

options.text: A side-by-side comparison of both options on business criteria such as cost per document, error rate on the pilot eval set, delivery time and operational risk.
An appendix with the full system prompts and tool schemas for both options, so the executives can judge the technical quality themselves.
Only the recommended option, presented in depth, so the committee isn't distracted by alternatives the team doesn't favour.
A clear statement of what the recommended option gives up, and the measurable signals that would prompt the team to revisit the decision.
An assurance that pinning the model version and freezing the prompts will make either option's outputs fully repeatable from run to run, which removes AI variability from the risk list.

questions.explanation: Decision-makers need options compared against credible alternatives, in their own terms (cost, quality, time, risk), and backed by eval data. They also need an honest account of the trade-off being accepted and of when it would be revisited. Together these make the decision informed and reversible. Anthropic's guidance frames the workflow-vs-agent choice as trading predictability and cost for flexibility, which is exactly the trade-off to make explicit, and expectations about variability should be set from measured eval results rather than from promises about configuration.

whyWrong.B: Raw prompts and schemas are the wrong level of detail for executives. They add noise without helping the business decision.
whyWrong.C: Hiding the alternatives stops the committee from seeing the trade-off and weakens trust in the recommendation.
whyWrong.E: Identical inputs can produce different outputs across API calls; Anthropic's glossary says this holds even with temperature set to 0, and newer models (Claude Opus 4.7 and later) reject any non-default temperature value outright. Variability is quantified with evals and managed with controls, not promised away.

questions.mindset: Compare credible options in business terms, and be explicit about what you are giving up.

questions.stem: A support agent that handles customer account data currently has a general web-fetch tool. The product lead wants to keep it because agents occasionally look up public shipping-carrier pages. Security and legal object that the tool could be used to send customer data to arbitrary URLs. The architect has to resolve the disagreement with a decision both sides can sign off on. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Keep the tool, add a system-prompt rule forbidding the agent from ever placing customer data in a URL or request body, show legal the new wording, and record that the risk has been mitigated.

Lay out the options (remove the tool, replace it with a narrow carrier-lookup tool, or gate it behind human approval) with each one's residual risk and cost, recommend the least-privilege option, and record security's sign-off.
Escalate to the CTO and ask for a ruling that product needs override the legal objection, pointing out that the tool is used only occasionally and that no data leak has actually occurred.

Keep the tool, log every fetched URL and its payload to a monitored dashboard that security reviews weekly, and tell legal that any misuse will be detected quickly and investigated under the existing incident process.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders disagree about a risk trade-off, the architect sets out the real options in business and risk terms, recommends one, and gets explicit sign-off from the accountable functions (security and legal) recorded in a decision log. On the merits, least privilege is the expected answer: Anthropic's guardrail guidance says to scope an agent's permissions as narrowly as possible so a successful injection can do minimal damage, which means replacing or removing broad capabilities rather than relying on instructions or after-the-fact detection. A narrow carrier-lookup tool also matches the advice to build a few targeted tools for the workflows you actually need.

whyWrong.A: A prompt instruction is guidance, not a control, and a prompt-injected agent can be talked out of it. Telling legal the risk is mitigated misrepresents the residual risk.
whyWrong.C: It turns a design trade-off into a political override and bypasses the functions accountable for data risk. 'No leak has happened yet' is not evidence that a credible exfiltration path is safe.
whyWrong.D: Logging detects misuse after the data has already left. It compensates for the risk instead of removing the capability that causes it.

questions.mindset: Bring risk trade-offs to the accountable owners with options and residual risk, and prefer the control that removes the capability.

questions.stem: An invoice-extraction pipeline currently meets its p95 latency target. The team has prototyped a second Claude verification pass that, on the eval set, cuts field-level errors substantially but roughly doubles per-document latency and cost. The finance operations director must decide whether to adopt it. How should the architect present the trade-off?

options.text: Recommend adopting the verification pass, because accuracy in finance always outweighs latency and cost, and present the latency increase as a minor technical detail that operations can absorb without discussion.
Recommend switching the whole pipeline to the largest available model instead of adding a pass, since a more capable model should cut errors without doubling latency or needing a second call.
Describe the verification pass as asking the model to double-check its own work, and tell the director that near-perfect extraction can be expected once it is added to the pipeline.

Quantify both options in the director's terms (errors per thousand invoices, the downstream cost of an error, p95 latency against the SLA, cost per invoice), then recommend one and let the director decide.

questions.explanation: Good trade-off communication puts eval-measured numbers into the business's own units, including what an error costs downstream and whether the SLA still holds. The architect then makes a recommendation and leaves the decision with the accountable owner. This uses the success criteria and eval data that Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends defining up front.

whyWrong.A: It skips the trade-off. Doubling latency may break the SLA, and 'always' isn't a business case.
whyWrong.B: It swaps a measured option for an unmeasured one. 'Use a bigger model' is a classic distractor that has no evidence behind it here.
whyWrong.C: It overpromises ('near-perfect') and misstates what the evidence shows. Expectations should be set from eval numbers.

questions.mindset: Express trade-offs in the decision-maker's units, using eval data, and let the owner decide.

questions.stem: A finance manager asks why the architect wants to restructure the prompts in a high-volume assistant so that a long, unchanging policy section always comes first. Which explanation is BOTH accurate and appropriate for a non-technical audience?

options.text: When many requests start with the same fixed text, the platform can reuse that already-processed opening instead of reprocessing it each time, which makes those requests cheaper and faster; the fixed part must come first for that to work.

Putting the policy first lets the platform store the answers it has already given and send them back whenever a similar question arrives, so we pay for each unique answer only once rather than every time it is asked by a customer.
Putting the policy first makes the model read it more carefully, which improves accuracy, and the platform automatically applies a discount to prompts that are well organised and clearly structured.
Putting the policy first makes every request after the first one in a session free, because the platform charges only for the first copy of any text it sees and nothing at all for repeats.

questions.explanation: Prompt caching reuses a processed prompt prefix, so a cache hit happens only when the start of the prompt is identical. Static content therefore goes first and variable content goes last. Cache reads are billed at a reduced rate and cut latency. The explanation is accurate and plain-language, and it doesn't overpromise.

whyWrong.B: Caching reuses the prompt prefix, not model outputs. Nothing returns stored answers.
whyWrong.C: It confuses caching with attention, and there is no discount for 'well-organised' prompts. The saving comes from reusing an identical prefix.
whyWrong.D: Overpromise. Cached reads are billed at a reduced rate, not free, the new tokens after the cached part are billed normally, and the cache expires after a few minutes without reuse (5 minutes by default).

questions.mindset: Explain mechanisms accurately in plain language, without overpromising.

questions.stem: The platform team proposes moving a production claims-summarisation service to a newer Claude model. Business owners are nervous because the current outputs are reviewed by adjusters every day, and a previous unannounced change caused complaints. Which TWO actions BEST communicate and manage this trade-off? Choose TWO.

options.text: Announce the upgrade as a pure improvement, because newer models score higher on public benchmarks, so a detailed comparison would only cause unnecessary concern.
Run the existing eval suite on both models and share the differences in summary quality, latency and cost per claim with the business owners before deciding.
Skip internal testing and rely on the provider's published benchmark results, since they cover far more tasks than the team's own eval set.
Keep the service pinned to the current model indefinitely, since any change carries risk and the adjusters are already used to its output style.
Propose a staged rollout with agreed success thresholds and a rollback path, and tell the adjusters what will change and when.

questions.explanation: Model changes are lifecycle events that should be justified with your own evals on your own task, then rolled out gradually against agreed thresholds, with a way back and clear communication to the affected users. That turns a feared change into a measured, reversible decision.

whyWrong.A: Public benchmarks don't measure this task, and leaving out a comparison repeats the surprise that already caused complaints.
whyWrong.C: Generic benchmarks don't replace task-specific evals. Anthropic's guidance is to define success criteria and test on your own representative cases.
whyWrong.D: Freezing forever ignores real benefits and eventual model deprecation. Risk should be managed with evals and a staged rollout, not avoided by never changing.

questions.mindset: Model changes are decided with your own evals and shipped gradually, with a rollback path and clear communication.

questions.stem: A platform team keeps its coding conventions for a monorepo (test commands, the error-handling pattern, the folder layout) on a wiki page. Developers using Claude Code report that generated code keeps ignoring these conventions. The team wants the guidance applied automatically for everyone who clones the repo, with minimal ongoing effort. What should the architect do?

options.text: Ask each developer to paste the wiki link into the first prompt of every Claude Code session so that the conventions are always in context.
Put the concise conventions in a project CLAUDE.md committed to the repository, and move area-specific rules into .claude/rules files scoped with paths patterns.
Put the conventions in the architect's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, since that file is loaded in every session and applies across all projects.
Expand the wiki page with more worked examples and announce it in the team channel each sprint, so that developers remember to point Claude at it when they start a session.

questions.explanation: Implementation guidance is useful only when it is actually applied. A project CLAUDE.md is shared through version control and loaded at the start of every session. Path-scoped .claude/rules files load only when Claude works with matching files, which keeps context lean. This puts the conventions where Claude reads them with no per-session effort.

whyWrong.A: It depends on manual effort in every session and will be applied inconsistently. It's the opposite of minimal ongoing effort.
whyWrong.C: User-level CLAUDE.md applies only to the architect's own machine. Teammates never receive it.
whyWrong.D: Improving the wiki doesn't change what Claude loads. The guidance stays out of the sessions where it's needed.

questions.mindset: Put implementation guidance where the tool loads it, and share it through version control.

questions.stem: An insurer's model-risk team must review a Claude-based assistant that drafts replies to policyholder complaints before it can go live. They ask the architect for documentation they can actually assess. Which document will BEST serve this review?

options.text: The model provider's published system card, usage policies and security certifications, presented as evidence that the assistant is safe and accurate enough for complaint handling.
A short benefits overview for the review team covering expected time savings, customer-satisfaction goals and the timeline for the rollout to all regions.
A system description: intended and out-of-scope uses, the data flow, the pinned model and how changes are approved, eval results with known limits, and where humans review outputs.
The full source code, system prompts and tool schemas for every component, with an offer to walk the reviewers through how each part of the assistant works, line by line.

questions.explanation: A review team needs a document that describes this system as deployed: what it is for and what it must not be used for, which data goes where, which model version it runs and how a change to it is controlled and re-evaluated, how well it actually performs on its own eval set (including known failure modes), and where a human checks or overrides the output. That lets reviewers judge risk against evidence. This is general documentation practice for AI systems (similar in spirit to a model card or system card, but for your application rather than the model), grounded in Anthropic's guidance to define success criteria and measure them with task-specific evals.

whyWrong.A: A provider's documentation describes the model in general, not this application, its data flow or its measured performance on complaints. Assurance has to come from evidence about the system as deployed.
whyWrong.B: It describes hoped-for benefits, not risks, limits or controls, so there is nothing for a risk review to assess.
whyWrong.D: Raw implementation detail is the wrong level. It doesn't state intended use, limits, measured performance or oversight points, so reviewers would have to reconstruct them.

questions.mindset: Document the system as deployed (use, data, model, evidence, oversight) for the people who must judge its risk.

questions.stem: An architect is handing a production document-triage agent over to a separate operations team that wasn't involved in building it. Which content should the handoff runbook prioritise?

options.text: Known failure modes and their symptoms, where logs and traces live, how to tell a 429 rate limit from a 529 overload and what to do for each, rollback steps, escalation contacts, and the eval dashboard for spotting drift.

The complete history of prompt iterations from development, with the eval score recorded for each version, so that operators understand every wording choice made during prompt tuning and can defend it if asked.
A conceptual explanation of how large language models generate tokens and why outputs can vary from run to run, so that operators are not alarmed by differences between otherwise identical requests.
A high-level architecture diagram of the components, data stores and their connections, which operators can use to reason about the system and work out procedures as issues come up.

questions.explanation: A runbook exists so operators can act without the original builders. It needs symptoms-to-action mappings, observability entry points, rollback and escalation paths, and quality monitoring. For Claude-based systems, that includes telling HTTP 429 (rate limit) apart from 529 (overloaded), since each needs a different response, and watching evals for drift after model or data changes.

whyWrong.B: A prompt history is a development artifact. It's long and doesn't tell an operator what to do when something breaks.
whyWrong.C: Background theory may help with understanding, but it isn't actionable operational guidance.
whyWrong.D: A diagram helps, but on its own it forces operators to improvise procedures during an incident, which is exactly what a runbook should prevent.

questions.mindset: Handoff docs are for acting: symptoms, signals, rollback, escalation.

questions.stem: A team is taking over maintenance of a retrieval-augmented HR policy assistant from the architect who designed it. When writing the architecture document for them, which TWO items are MOST important to include? Choose TWO.

options.text: The exact model version string in use, described as a permanent design constraint that the new team must not change.
A catalogue of every prompt variant tried during development, including the ones that were abandoned, with notes on why each was dropped.
The end-to-end data flow: which employee data is sent to which services, where it is stored, for how long, and who has access to it.
The vendor's published benchmark scores, as evidence that the assistant's chosen model is accurate enough for HR policy questions.
The ingestion and re-indexing process: where each policy comes from, who approves updates, and when and how the index is rebuilt.

questions.explanation: Maintainers need to know where sensitive data goes, because governance follows the data flow rather than the contract. They also need to know how the knowledge base is kept current: in a retrieval-augmented assistant, answer quality depends on the index holding the right, current documents, and a policy refresh that is half-applied or skipped is a classic cause of confident but outdated answers. Both items describe how the system actually runs, which is what a new team must keep working.

whyWrong.A: Model versions change and are eventually deprecated. Documenting one as permanent creates a false constraint; document how a model change is validated instead.
whyWrong.B: An exhaustive history of discarded variants is noise. Key rationale belongs in a short decision record.
whyWrong.D: Generic benchmarks don't show how this assistant performs on HR policy questions. Only your own evals do.

questions.mindset: Document how data and knowledge move through the system, and leave out history and trivia.

questions.stem: An architect is writing a prompt-authoring guide for six product teams moving their agents to a current Claude model. Many existing system prompts are full of unexplained rules such as 'CRITICAL: You MUST call the search tool before every answer.' Since the move, teams report agents calling tools far more often than the task needs. What should the guide tell the teams to do?

options.text: Repeat each critical rule at both the start and the end of the system prompt, in capital letters, so that the new model cannot miss or misread any of them.
Pin the agents back to the older model, because prompts are tuned to one specific model and should stay frozen together with it for as long as that model remains available.
Add several few-shot examples that show the search tool being called before every single answer, so that tool use stays predictable and consistent across all six teams' agents.
Rewrite rules in plain language with the reason behind each (such as when a search is really needed), then re-run each team's evals on tool-call rates before rollout.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's prompting best practices note that recent models follow system-prompt instructions more closely than older ones, so emphatic wording that was added to stop older models under-using a tool can now make them over-use it. The advice is to dial the aggressive language back to normal phrasing ('Use this tool when...'). The same guide recommends explaining the motivation behind an instruction so Claude can apply it with judgment. Because the change affects behaviour, teams should confirm it with their own evals before rolling it out.

whyWrong.A: More emphasis is the cause of the over-triggering, not the cure. It pushes the new model further toward calling the tool every time.
whyWrong.B: It avoids the problem rather than fixing it, and older models are eventually deprecated and retired, so the prompts will have to be updated anyway.
whyWrong.C: Examples that call the tool every time teach exactly the behaviour the teams are trying to remove.

questions.mindset: Implementation guidance should explain the why in normal language, and changes to it are checked with evals.

questions.stem: An internal platform team publishes an MCP server whose tools will be called by agents built by several other teams. A thorough README for developers already exists. What is the MOST effective way to make sure those agents use the tools correctly?

options.text: Keep tool names and descriptions as short as possible to save tokens on every call, and ask consuming teams to copy the README's guidance into their own system prompts where it is needed.

Write detailed descriptions and parameter documentation in the tool definitions themselves (when to use each tool, input formats, important limits), because that is what the model reads when choosing and calling tools.
Rely on the model to infer correct usage from the tool and parameter names, since current models are good at guessing a tool's purpose from a descriptive identifier and a typed schema.

Publish the README on the internal developer portal and require each consuming team to complete a short training session and a sign-off checklist before they are allowed to connect their agents to the server.

questions.explanation: For an agent, the tool definition is the documentation. Anthropic's tool-use docs say detailed descriptions are the most important factor in tool-use performance, and 'Writing effective tools for agents' recommends writing them as you would for a new teammate. A README for humans doesn't reach the model.

whyWrong.A: Terse descriptions hurt tool selection, and copying guidance into many system prompts duplicates it and lets it drift.
whyWrong.C: Names alone are ambiguous. The docs explicitly recommend detailed descriptions.
whyWrong.D: Training the developers doesn't change what their agents read at runtime.

questions.mindset: For agents, the tool description is the documentation.

questions.stem: An architect is writing the implementation guide for teams building an extraction pipeline that uses structured outputs with a strict JSON schema. Which statement should the guide include so that teams build the pipeline correctly?

options.text: Because the schema is enforced by the API, every extracted value is guaranteed to be correct, so downstream validation code can be removed to reduce latency and simplify the pipeline for the teams.
If an extracted record looks wrong, ask the model in a follow-up turn to re-verify its own answer, because self-checking guarantees that the final values are accurate and complete.
Schema enforcement guarantees that the response's shape conforms to the schema, but not that the values are right, so business-rule checks such as totals matching line items must stay in code.
Retry each request until the output passes all business rules, with no retry limit, because the model will eventually produce a fully correct record if it is given enough attempts.

questions.explanation: Structured outputs constrain the response to match the supplied JSON schema, which removes parsing and shape errors. They don't make the content semantically correct. Implementation guidance must keep deterministic business validation in code (with bounded retries or human review) and say clearly what the schema does and doesn't guarantee.

whyWrong.A: It mistakes syntactic guarantees for semantic ones, so invalid values flow downstream.
whyWrong.B: Self-checking may catch some errors, but it guarantees nothing, and the model can confidently confirm a wrong value. 'Ask the model to self-check' is a classic distractor where a code gate belongs.
whyWrong.D: Unbounded retries risk runaway cost and latency, and they never terminate if the source document is genuinely ambiguous. Retries need a cap and an escalation path.

questions.mindset: Document what a control guarantees and what it doesn't; schemas fix shape, code checks meaning.

questions.stem: Over a year of iterations on a Claude-based claims system (prompt changes, a model upgrade, a new retrieval index), the architecture documents have drifted from the running system, and new engineers no longer trust them. Which TWO practices BEST keep architecture documentation accurate over time? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have one senior engineer rewrite all architecture documents each quarter from memory and from interviews with the team.
Store the architecture docs and decision records in the repository, and update them in the same pull request as the change they describe, as part of review.
At each release, regenerate the entire documentation set automatically with Claude from the codebase and publish it immediately with no human review, so the docs can never lag behind the code.
When a significant decision changes, write a new decision record that supersedes the old one instead of silently editing it, so the history of reasoning is kept.
Keep a separate copy of the architecture document for each stakeholder group, tailored to its interests, and update each copy independently.

questions.explanation: Docs-as-code ties documentation updates to the change itself, so the review process catches drift. Superseding decision records follows the original ADR convention: when a decision is reversed, keep the old record and mark it superseded, because it is still relevant to know what the decision was and that it no longer applies. Both are general architecture practices that keep implementation guidance trustworthy across lifecycle iterations; Claude Code's own guidance similarly keeps shared instructions in version control and asks teams to review them periodically for outdated or conflicting content.

whyWrong.A: Periodic rewrites from memory let drift build up between cycles and depend on a single person.
whyWrong.C: AI-assisted drafting is useful, but unreviewed regeneration can introduce errors and loses decision rationale that isn't visible in code.
whyWrong.E: Separately maintained copies multiply drift. Tailor views from one source of truth instead.

questions.mindset: Docs change with the code they describe, and decisions are superseded, never silently overwritten.
